Fifteen jobs, sixty-one named patterns, and a Record column that says where every name comes from — this is the row list the whole series refers back to.

The same menu as the previous chapter, laid out as a table: fifteen jobs, sixty-one named ways of doing them, with a note on where each name comes from — Richardson’s published index, a companion from an older book, or one of the two forms of the saga. It is the row list the rest of the series refers back to, and the maps below draw it in one picture so the shape of the language can be seen before the tables are read.

runs.t: This is the working catalog for the research.

It has 15 categories. 53 patterns are on Chris Richardson’s published index at microservices.io/patterns/index.html. Sidecar and service mesh have their own pattern pages on that site and are included here, which brings his named patterns to 55.
Saga choreography and saga orchestration are the two forms of the saga, not extra index entries.
Timeout, retry, bulkhead, and ambassador are companion patterns that teams use for the same jobs. They are marked so they are not mistaken for index entries.
The “Record” column says where the name comes from.
Index
means the published pattern-language index.
Pattern page
means a page on microservices.io that the index listing does not currently show. Form of saga means one of the two ways a saga is coordinated.
Companion
means a pattern from Michael Nygard’s Release It! (2007) or from the Azure Architecture Center that belongs in the same category.
General cloud patterns that are not part of this language — sharding, leader election, competing consumers, and the rest of the Azure cloud design catalog — are left out.
They solve infrastructure problems that a microservice system may also have, and they are not the microservice pattern language.

rows: Which architectural style the application uses.
How the application is cut into services.
How a running system is replaced without a single cutover.
How a command or a query is carried out when the data lives in more than one service.
Publishing a message with the database write
How a service avoids writing to its database and then failing to publish the event.
The mechanism one service uses to talk to another, or to an external client.
How clients outside the system reach the services.
How a caller learns the current network address of a service that may have many instances.
How a failing or slow dependency is stopped from taking down its callers.
How the service that handles a request knows who asked.
How operators reconstruct what a request did after it has crossed several services.
The unit that is started, stopped, and scaled.
Where logging, configuration, discovery, and traffic policy live, so each service does not rebuild them.
How a service is checked without standing up the whole system.
Composing a screen from many services
How a page that needs data from several services is assembled.

runs.t: Which architectural style the application uses.

rows: One deployable unit holds the user interface, the domain logic, and the database.
The application is a set of independently deployable, loosely coupled services.

runs.t: How the application is cut into services.

rows: Each service corresponds to a business capability, such as order management or delivery.
Each service corresponds to a domain-driven-design subdomain and its bounded context.
The service boundary follows the team that owns the capability.
A service handles a synchronous request without waiting for another service to respond.

runs.t: How a running system is replaced without a single cutover.

rows: New behavior is built beside the old system, and a facade routes each request to one or the other, until the old system can be retired.
A translation layer keeps a new service’s model from being bent by the legacy system it still calls.

runs.t: How a command or a query is carried out when the data lives in more than one service.

rows: Each service has a private database. Other services reach that data only through its API or its events.
Several services read and write the same database schema.
A business action is a sequence of local transactions. If a later step fails, earlier steps run compensating actions.
A form of the saga. Each service publishes an event, and the next service reacts. No coordinator holds the whole workflow.
A form of the saga. One coordinator tells each participant the next step and runs compensations.
The service that performs a command keeps a read-only copy of data it does not own, updated from events.
A query calls the services that own the data and joins the answers in memory.
Commands update the service database. Queries read one or more materialized views maintained for that purpose.
A service publishes an event whenever its data changes, so other services can react.
The service stores an aggregate as the sequence of events that produced it, and rebuilds current state from that log.

blocks.text: Publishing a message with the database write

runs.t: How a service avoids writing to its database and then failing to publish the event.

rows: The service writes the business row and an outbox row in the same local transaction. A separate process publishes the outbox.
A process reads the database transaction log and publishes the changes it finds there.
A process polls a table of events or outbox rows and publishes any that have not yet been sent.

runs.t: The mechanism one service uses to talk to another, or to an external client.

rows: A caller sends a request and waits for a response, typically over HTTP or gRPC.
Services exchange asynchronous messages through a broker. The sender does not have to be running at the same moment as the consumer.
Services speak a protocol built for that domain, rather than a general HTTP or messaging API.
A message handler can safely receive the same message more than once and still produce one effect.

runs.t: How clients outside the system reach the services.

rows: One entry service routes, and sometimes aggregates, calls so clients do not have to know the internal services.
A separate API gateway for each kind of client, owned with that client. One experience, one backend.

runs.t: How a caller learns the current network address of a service that may have many instances.

rows: The caller queries a registry and chooses an instance.
The caller hits a router at a stable address. The router queries a registry and forwards the request.
A database of service instances and their locations. Callers or routers query it.
Each service instance registers and unregisters itself with the registry.
A registrar, such as the platform, registers and unregisters instances on their behalf.

runs.t: How a failing or slow dependency is stopped from taking down its callers.

rows: A proxy fails calls immediately once the remote failure rate crosses a threshold, then allows a few trial calls later.
A caller stops waiting after a set time, so a slow dependency cannot hold its threads.
A caller repeats a failed call a limited number of times, usually only when the failure is safe to repeat.
The caller isolates the threads, connections, or pool used for one dependency, so that dependency cannot exhaust the caller.

runs.t: How the service that handles a request knows who asked.

rows: A token that carries the caller’s identity travels with the request from service to service.

runs.t: How operators reconstruct what a request did after it has crossed several services.

rows: Service logs are shipped to one store so they can be searched together.
Each service records counts, timings, and other statistics about its operations.
User actions are recorded in a durable store for later review.
Each external request gets an identifier that is passed between services, and each hop records its start and end.
Exceptions are reported to a central tracker that groups them and notifies developers.
A service exposes an endpoint that a monitor can call to learn whether it can take work.
Deploys and configuration changes are recorded so they can be lined up with incidents.

runs.t: The unit that is started, stopped, and scaled.

rows: Several service instances share one machine or one operating system.
Each service instance runs on its own host.
Each service instance is packaged as its own virtual machine.
Each service instance runs in its own container. This became the ordinary choice after Docker and Kubernetes.
The platform runs the service on demand, and the team does not manage the host.
An automated platform deploys services and presents them as a service abstraction, as Kubernetes does.

runs.t: Where logging, configuration, discovery, and traffic policy live, so each service does not rebuild them.

rows: A framework handles the cross-cutting concerns and leaves the team to write the domain logic.
Database locations, credentials, and feature flags live outside the service package.
A copyable starter service already contains the build and the standard cross-cutting concerns.
Cross-cutting concerns run in a process or container beside the service instance.
A mesh mediates communication in and out of each service, and carries configuration, logs, health, metrics, and tracing.
An outbound proxy beside the service handles connectivity, retries, and monitoring for calls that service makes.

runs.t: How a service is checked without standing up the whole system.

rows: The team that calls a service writes a test suite that states the contract it depends on.
A client verifies that it can still speak to the service it calls.
A service is tested in isolation, with test doubles standing in for the services it calls.

blocks.text: Composing a screen from many services

runs.t: How a page that needs data from several services is assembled.

rows: The server builds the page from HTML fragments, each generated by the service that owns that part of the business.
The client builds the screen from UI fragments, each rendered by a component tied to one business capability.

runs.t: Sources: Chris Richardson, pattern language index and pattern pages, microservices.io, consulted 29 September 2026. Saga: Hector Garcia-Molina and Kenneth Salem, “Sagas,” SIGMOD 1987; choreography and orchestration as described by Richardson, Azure Architecture Center, and AWS Prescriptive Guidance. Circuit breaker, timeout, retry, and bulkhead: Michael Nygard, Release It! (2007); circuit breaker is also the reliability pattern on the index. Ambassador: Azure Architecture Center. Strangler application: Martin Fowler. Anti-corruption layer: Eric Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2003). Backend for frontend: Phil Calçado’s name for the SoundCloud practice; Sam Newman’s pattern write-up.

blocks.title: Read it again: three things to carry away

paragraphs.t: Fifteen jobs, sixty-one patterns, and a Record column that says where each name comes from.
Companions — timeout, retry, bulkhead, ambassador — are marked so they are not mistaken for index entries.
General cloud patterns are deliberately left out; they are not the microservice pattern language.
